section.title: Chapter review and discovery problems
section.p: Chapter 1 began with motion. It asked how to pass between velocity and distance, slope and area, difference and sum.

Chapter 2 built the language that this question needs. We used the real line to measure nearness, functions to record dependence, graphs to see geometric behavior, and models to connect formulas with real applications. We also learned that a graph on a screen is only evidence, not proof.
The next chapter returns to the original motion problem. But now we are ready to say what “near” means.

exercise.title: What language did this chapter build for the word near?

statement.p: The real line turns numbers into points and distances; completeness says the line has no gaps. In your own words, why does a limit need both a language of closeness such as |A-T|<\varepsilon and an unbroken number line for the destination of a limiting process?

hint.p: Inequalities control error. Completeness guarantees that the number those shrinking errors are aiming at actually exists.

exercise.title: Why is a graph on a screen only evidence?

statement.p: Chapter 2 used graphs to see shape, sign, roots, and models, but also warned that a screen picture is made with a window and a finite sample. In your own words, what should a graph be trusted to do, and what must still be checked by algebra, definitions, or modeling assumptions?

hint.p: A picture can suggest a pattern. It cannot, by itself, prove that the pattern holds for every allowed input, or that the model still makes sense outside the data.

subsection.title: Hook: limits make near into mathematics
subsection.p: The last problem is the doorway to the next chapter.
the average velocity from t=2 to t=2+h is
As h gets close to 0, the average velocity gets close to 4. Chapter 2 gave us the language to make that sentence sharper:
So if we want the output error to be less than \varepsilon, we can demand
This is the shape of a limit. The input is allowed to approach a forbidden or special value. The output is forced into any desired error bound.
The next chapter gives this idea its name.

exercise.title: What is already the shape of a limit?

statement.p: For s(t)=t^2, the average velocity from t=2 to t=2+h is 4+h with h\neq0, and the error from 4 is exactly |h|. In your own words, what promise is already visible here, and why is the input allowed to approach a forbidden value while the output is forced into any desired error bound?

hint.p: The condition 0<|h|<\varepsilon keeps the step away from zero and still small enough. That is the measuring-tape language the next chapter will name.
